Eating disorders – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Anorexia, bulimia and binge-eating disorder: a troubled relationship with food and the body.
Eating
🍽️ Eating disorders

They are serious mental health problems, not whims or a matter of willpower. They include food restriction, binge eating and compensatory behaviours, and excessive concern about weight and body image.
Food restriction or intense fear of gaining weight
Binge eating followed by guilt and compensatory behaviours
Constant preoccupation with weight and body
Avoiding eating in public, ritualising meals
Isolation, mood changes, tiredness

Myth: They only affect teenage girls.
Fact: They can affect people of any age and gender.

Myth: It is a fad or a matter of vanity.
Fact: They are serious disorders with risks to physical and mental health.
The sooner help is sought, the better the outlook. See someone if there is significant weight loss, dizziness, loss of periods or compensatory behaviours.
It requires a multidisciplinary approach: doctor, psychologist, psychiatrist and dietitian. In teenagers, the family is a key part of treatment.
Don’t comment on weight or body, for better or for worse.
Don’t force them to eat; look for professional help.
Keep family meals a calm space.
Schizophrenia and psychotic disorders – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Changes in how reality is perceived: hallucinations, delusions and disorganised thinking.
Psychosis
🌀 Schizophrenia and psychotic disorders
Psychosis involves a loss of contact with reality. Schizophrenia is one of the best-known psychotic disorders. With appropriate treatment, many people lead full lives.
Hearing voices or seeing things others do not perceive
Fixed ideas that do not follow logic (delusions)
Disorganised thinking and speech
Social withdrawal, apathy, lack of motivation
Neglecting hygiene or usual activities

Myth: Schizophrenia is “split personality”.
Fact: It is not: they are completely different conditions.

Myth: People with schizophrenia are violent.
Fact: The vast majority are not; they are more often victims than aggressors.
After a first psychotic episode or a sudden change in behaviour, an urgent psychiatric assessment is needed. Early intervention improves the outlook.
Antipsychotic treatment prescribed by psychiatry, combined with psychoeducation, therapy and social and work support.
Don’t argue about the content of delusions; be present and calm.
Help them stay on their treatment.
Look for support groups for families.
Borderline personality disorder – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Intense emotional instability, in relationships and in one’s self-image.
Personality
🎭 Borderline personality disorder
It is marked by very intense emotions that change quickly, fear of abandonment, unstable relationships and impulsivity. It is a treatable disorder with a good outlook given the right support.
Intense fear of being abandoned
Intense, unstable relationships
Rapid mood changes
Chronic feeling of emptiness
Impulsivity or self-harming behaviours
Anger that is hard to control

Myth: They are manipulative people.
Fact: They often feel enormous emotional pain and use the strategies they have.

Myth: They can’t be treated.
Fact: Specific therapies such as DBT have good results.
If unstable emotions or relationships cause you ongoing distress, or there is self-harm.
Specific psychotherapies: dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), mentalisation-based therapy, among others.
Validate their emotions without validating every behaviour.
Set clear, kind limits.
Look for support for yourself: caring for someone is demanding.
ADHD (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Persistent difficulties with attention, hyperactivity and/or impulsivity.
Neurodevelopment
⚡ ADHD (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder)
It is a neurodevelopmental disorder that appears in childhood and can continue into adulthood. It is not a lack of upbringing or willpower.
Difficulty sustaining attention
Frequent distraction, forgetfulness
Restlessness, difficulty sitting still
Impulsivity
Disorganisation and difficulty managing time

Myth: It is a modern invention or an excuse.
Fact: It has been described and researched for decades.

Myth: It only affects children.
Fact: Many adults have it undiagnosed, especially women.
If symptoms affect school, work or relationships on an ongoing basis.
Multimodal intervention: psychoeducation, adjustments at school or work, behavioural therapy and, where appropriate, medication prescribed by a specialist.
Build routines and break tasks into steps.
Reward effort, not just results.
Avoid negative labels (“lazy”, “scatterbrained”).
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
A different way of communicating, relating and perceiving the world.
🧩 Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition. Every person is different: support needs can vary widely. It is not an illness that needs to be “cured”.
Differences in communication and social interaction
Intense, specific interests
Need for routine and difficulty with change
Sensory sensitivity (noises, textures, lights)

Myth: Autism can be cured with diets or vaccines.
Fact: There is no evidence: vaccines do not cause autism.

Myth: Autistic people have no emotions.
Fact: They feel them, often very intensely, but may express them differently.
If you suspect that you or someone close to you could be autistic, contact a specialist service for an assessment.
Autism is not treated as such; instead, support is offered: early intervention, speech therapy, educational and workplace adjustments and treatment of associated conditions (anxiety, depression).
Respect their sensory and routine needs.
Prepare them for changes in good time.
Focus on strengths and interests.
Addictions and problematic use – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Loss of control over substance use or behaviours (gambling, screens...).
Addictions
🔗 Addictions and problematic use
Addiction is a chronic, treatable illness. It is marked by difficulty controlling use despite negative consequences.
Using more than planned or for longer
Failed attempts to cut down or stop
Tolerance and withdrawal
Neglecting obligations and relationships
Continuing despite the problems it causes

Myth: You just need willpower to stop.
Fact: Addiction affects brain circuits; it usually needs professional support.

Myth: You have to “hit rock bottom” before asking for help.
Fact: The sooner you ask for help, the better.
If you feel you have lost control of your use or you are worried about someone close to you.
Individualised approach: outpatient care (CAS), motivational and cognitive behavioural therapy, mutual-help groups and, in some cases, medication or inpatient treatment.
Speak out of concern, without reproach.
Set clear limits and stick to them.
Look for support for yourself in family groups.
Insomnia and sleep problems – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Difficulty sleeping that affects daily life.
Sleep
🌙 Insomnia and sleep problems
Sleep and mental health are closely linked: sleeping badly can worsen mood and anxiety, and vice versa.
Difficulty falling asleep or frequent waking
Waking too early
Tiredness during the day
Irritability and difficulty concentrating

Myth: You must always sleep 8 hours.
Fact: Needs vary from person to person.

Myth: Pills are the solution.
Fact: For chronic insomnia, therapy is the first-line treatment.
If insomnia lasts more than three nights a week for over a month.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended treatment. Sleep hygiene measures: regular schedules, avoiding screens and caffeine before bed, a dark, cool bedroom.
Respect their schedules and rest.
Avoid turning sleep into a source of pressure.
Grief and loss – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
A natural process of reacting to a loss, which may need support.
🕯️ Grief and loss
Grief is the normal reaction to losing a loved one or an important situation. It has no timetable or rigid stages. Everyone experiences it in their own way.
Sadness, longing, crying
Anger, guilt, anxiety
Difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep and appetite
Feeling unreal or isolated

Myth: You have to get over it within a set time.
Fact: There is no deadline: every grief is unique.

Myth: Crying is a sign of weakness.
Fact: Emotional expression is part of healing.
If after many months the pain is so intense that you cannot live normally, or you have thoughts of wanting to die to be reunited with the person you lost.
Support in grief groups, psychotherapy focused on complicated grief when needed, and social support.
Support them with your presence, not with stock phrases.
Talk about the person who has died if they wish.
Offer practical help (meals, errands).
Self-harm and suicidal thoughts – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
If you are thinking of harming yourself right now, you are not alone: ask for help now.
Risk and crisis
🤝 Self-harm and suicidal thoughts
Suicidal thoughts and self-harm are forms of very intense emotional pain. They are more common than people think and they can be treated. You can feel better, even if it doesn’t seem so right now.
Feeling there is no way out or being a burden
Thoughts of death or of wanting to disappear
Saying goodbye, giving away belongings, sudden changes in behaviour
Self-harm as a way of coping with emotional pain

Myth: Talking about it gives people ideas.
Fact: Asking directly and calmly helps and does not increase the risk.

Myth: People who talk about it don’t do it.
Fact: Every comment must be taken seriously.
If right now you are thinking of harming yourself or ending your life, call 112 (emergencies) or 024 (suicide prevention line, free, 24 h) now. If you can, don’t stay alone.
Urgent or priority professional assessment, a safety plan, psychotherapy (CBT, DBT) and, if needed, medication. Recovery is possible.
Ask directly and calmly: “Are you thinking of harming yourself?”.
Listen without judging and don’t promise to keep it secret.
Don’t leave them alone if there is immediate risk, and call 112.
Specific phobias – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Intense, out-of-proportion fear of a specific thing or situation (animals, heights, blood, flying...).
🕷️ Specific phobias

A specific phobia is a very intense fear of a particular object or situation that almost always appears on encountering it and is clearly out of proportion to the real danger. The person avoids it or endures it with great distress. They are among the most common fears and respond best to treatment.
Immediate fear or distress when faced with the trigger (or even just thinking about it)
Palpitations, sweating, trembling, feeling breathless or dizzy
Avoiding situations (flying, driving, going to the dentist, seeing blood...)
Planning life so as not to meet what is feared
Knowing the fear is exaggerated and still being unable to control it

Myth: It is an exaggeration or a lack of willpower.
Fact: Fear is an automatic response of the body. It is not solved by “trying harder”, but it is by gradual exposure.

Myth: If I face it all at once, it will go away.
Fact: Sudden exposure without preparation can reinforce the fear. It works better when gradual and agreed in advance.
When avoidance limits work, studies, health (e.g. not going to the doctor) or relationships, or when the fear causes you significant distress.
The treatment of choice is cognitive behavioural therapy with gradual exposure, often in just a few sessions. Medication is not usually the first resort.
Don’t make fun of them or compare it to your own fear: for them it is real.
Don’t force them to face it all at once, but don’t help them avoid everything either.
Celebrate small steps forward and respect the pace of exposure.
Complex PTSD and ongoing trauma – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Effects of repeated or prolonged trauma, often from childhood: beyond memories, it affects how you see yourself and relate to others.
🧩 Complex PTSD and ongoing trauma

Complex trauma refers to repeated or prolonged experiences that are hard to escape (abuse, neglect, violence). In addition to PTSD symptoms, ICD-11 describes complex PTSD with difficulty regulating emotions, a negative self-image and problems maintaining close relationships.
Intrusive memories, nightmares or flashbacks
Avoiding people, places or conversations that recall what happened
